intro.title: Patterns: regular expressions
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`includes` can tell you whether text contains `"cat"`. But what about "contains a number", "is a valid postcode" or "find every hashtag"? For those you describe a **pattern**, with a **regular expression** (regex for short). In JavaScript you write one between slashes: `/cat/`.

```
const pattern = /\d+/
console.log(pattern.test("Room 42"))
console.log(pattern.test("No numbers here"))
console.log("Room 42, floor 3".match(pattern)[0])
```

**`pattern.test(text)`** says whether the text matches anywhere. **`text.match(pattern)`** gives the first match (or `null`). With the **`g`** flag (global), `match` gives a list of **all** matches. The **`i`** flag ignores case.

The building blocks:

| Pattern | Matches |
|---|---|
| `\d` | a digit 0–9 |
| `\w` | a letter, digit or `_` |
| `\s` | a space, tab or new line |
| `.` | any one character |
| `[aeiou]` | one of these |
| `[^aeiou]` | anything but these |
| `[a-z]` | a range |

And how many:

| After a piece | Means |
|---|---|
| `+` | one or more |
| `*` | zero or more |
| `?` | optional |
| `{3}` | exactly 3 |
| `{2,4}` | 2 to 4 |

**`^`** at the start and **`$`** at the end tie the pattern to the start and end of the text, so the **whole** text must fit, which is what you want for checking input:

```
const pin = /^\d{4}$/
console.log(pin.test("2580"))
console.log(pin.test("25800"))
console.log(pin.test("ab12"))
console.log("Tea, TEA and tea".match(/tea/gi))
```

To match a character that has a special meaning, like `.` or `?`, put a backslash before it: `/\./` matches a real dot. Regexes are powerful but get hard to read quickly: keep them short, and test them on good **and** bad examples.

intro.title: Groups, matchAll and replace
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Finding a pattern is good; pulling **pieces** out of it is better. Brackets `( )` in a regex make a **group**: the part of the match it covers is kept for you, numbered from 1.

```
const m = "Date: 2026-11-12".match(/(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})/)
console.log(m[0])
console.log(m[1], m[2], m[3])
```

`m[0]` is the whole match; `m[1]`, `m[2]`… are the groups. Numbers are easy to mix up, so you can **name** groups with `(?<name>…)` and read them from `m.groups`:

```
const m = "Ana Lima <ana@example.com>".match(/(?<name>[^<]+) <(?<email>[^>]+)>/)
console.log(m.groups.name.trim(), "/", m.groups.email)
```

With the `g` flag, `match` gives only the whole matches and loses the groups. To go through every match **with** its groups, use **`text.matchAll(pattern)`** (the pattern must have `g`) in a `for…of` loop:

```
const text = "apples=3, pears=5, plums=12"
for (const m of text.matchAll(/(\w+)=(\d+)/g)) {
  console.log(m[1], "→", Number(m[2]))
}
```

**`replace`** and **`replaceAll`** take a regex too. In the new text, `$1`, `$2` stand for the groups. Or pass a **function**: it gets the match and the groups and returns what to put instead, which lets you change each match differently.

```
console.log("2026-11-12".replace(/(\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+)/, "$3/$2/$1"))
console.log("I have 3 cats and 2 dogs".replace(/\d+/g, (n) => n * 2))
console.log("too    many   spaces".replace(/\s+/g, " "))
```

intro.title: Cleaning messy text
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Text that comes from people is messy: extra spaces, odd capitals, blank lines, `"Yes"`, `"yes "` and `"Y"` all meaning the same. Before you can count, compare or search it, you **clean** it, the same way every time.

A cleaning function usually does a few small steps in a row, each one simple:

```
function cleanName(raw) {
  return raw
    .trim()
    .replace(/\s+/g, " ")
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/\b\w/g, (c) => c.toUpperCase())
}
console.log(cleanName("   aNA    maria   lima "))
```

For text with many lines, **split** it into lines with `split("\n")` (or `split(/\r?\n/)`, which also handles the Windows line ending `\r\n`), clean each line, and **drop** the blank ones with `filter`.

```
const raw = "milk\n\n  bread \r\nEGGS\n   \n"
const items = raw
  .split(/\r?\n/)
  .map((line) => line.trim().toLowerCase())
  .filter((line) => line !== "")
console.log(items)
```

To compare words fairly, make a **key**: the cleaned form used only for comparing. `"Café"` and `"cafe"` differ only by an accent; `normalize("NFD")` splits an accented letter into the letter and its accent, and removing the accents (the range `\u0300-\u036f`) leaves plain letters.

```
const key = (word) => word.normalize("NFD").replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, "").toLowerCase()
console.log(key("Café") === key("cafe"))
```

A **slug** is a cleaned name used in web addresses, like `my-first-post`: small letters and digits, with dashes between words. And always keep the **original** text too: cleaning throws information away, and you may need it later.

intro.title: JSON: data as text
intro.bodyMarkdown:
**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is the way most programs swap data: servers send it, apps save settings in it, files store it. It looks almost like JavaScript objects and arrays, with a few strict rules.

```text
{
  "name": "Ana",
  "age": 31,
  "tags": ["admin", "editor"],
  "address": { "city": "Lisbon" },
  "active": true,
  "manager": null
}
```

The rules: keys **must** be in double quotes; text uses double quotes; no comments; no trailing commas; values are only text, numbers, `true`, `false`, `null`, arrays and objects. **No** functions, `undefined`, dates or `NaN`.

**`JSON.stringify(value)`** turns a value into JSON text, and **`JSON.parse(text)`** turns JSON text back into a value. `stringify` can lay the text out nicely: its third argument is the indent.

```
const user = { name: "Ana", tags: ["admin"], active: true }
const text = JSON.stringify(user)
console.log(text)
console.log(JSON.stringify(user, null, 2))
const back = JSON.parse(text)
console.log(back.tags[0])
```

Watch what gets lost: properties that are `undefined` or functions **vanish**, `NaN` becomes `null`, and a `Date` becomes text. Parsing gives you a **plain** object, not an instance of your class: that is why the Classes quest had `toJSON` and `fromJSON`.

```
const odd = { a: undefined, b: NaN, c: () => 1, d: new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 2)) }
console.log(JSON.stringify(odd))
```

`JSON.parse` **throws** a `SyntaxError` on bad text, so wrap it in `try`…`catch` when the text comes from outside. Its second argument, a **reviver**, can fix values on the way in, like turning date text back into `Date`s. `stringify`'s second argument can be a list of the keys to keep.

intro.title: Dates and times
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Birthdays, deadlines, opening hours, "posted 3 days ago": programs are full of dates. JavaScript keeps them in **`Date`** objects. `new Date()` is right now; `new Date(year, monthIndex, day)` is a day of your choice.

```
const launch = new Date(2026, 2, 14)
console.log(launch.getFullYear(), launch.getMonth(), launch.getDate())
console.log(launch.getDay())
```

Two old surprises: **months count from 0** (January is 0, March is 2, December is 11), but days of the month count from 1. And `getDay()` is the day of the **week**, from 0 (Sunday) to 6 (Saturday); `getDate()` is the day of the month.

Under the hood a date is one number: the **milliseconds** since 1 January 1970. `date.getTime()` gives it, and subtracting two dates gives the milliseconds between them. Divide by `1000 * 60 * 60 * 24` for days; round it, because a clock change for summer time can make a day 23 or 25 hours long.

```
const DAY = 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24
const today = new Date(2026, 10, 12)
const holiday = new Date(2026, 11, 24)
console.log(Math.round((holiday - today) / DAY), "days to go")
```

To move a date, change a part with a `set` method. JavaScript rolls over for you: day 32 of January is 1 February. Make a **copy** first (`new Date(date)`), because the `set` methods change the date itself.

```
const start = new Date(2026, 0, 30)
const later = new Date(start)
later.setDate(later.getDate() + 5)
console.log(later.getMonth(), later.getDate())
console.log(start.getDate())
```

Dates and time zones are tricky. `new Date(2026, 0, 30)` is midnight **where the computer is**. Text in ISO form like `"2026-01-30T09:00:00Z"` (`Z` meaning UTC, world time) is the same moment everywhere, and `toISOString()` writes a date that way. Store and send dates in ISO form; turn them into local time only to show them.

intro.title: Formatting for people: Intl
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Numbers and dates look different around the world. One and a quarter thousand is written `1,250.5` in the US, `1.250,5` in Germany and `1 250,5` in France; dates may be day first or month first. Writing this by hand is error-prone. JavaScript has it built in: **`Intl`**, the internationalisation tools.

**`Intl.NumberFormat(locale, options)`** makes a formatter; its `format(n)` gives the text. The **locale** is a language and region code like `"en-US"`, `"en-GB"`, `"de-DE"` or `"pt-BR"`.

```
const n = 1234567.891
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US").format(n))
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("de-DE").format(n))
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { maximumFractionDigits: 1 }).format(n))
```

Options pick the style. `style: "currency"` with a `currency` code gives money with the right symbol and decimals; `style: "percent"` turns `0.25` into `25%`; `notation: "compact"` gives `1.2M`.

```
const price = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" })
console.log(price.format(1234.5))
const euro = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IE", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" })
console.log(euro.format(9.9))
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "percent" }).format(0.256))
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { notation: "compact" }).format(1234567))
```

Dates work the same with **`Intl.DateTimeFormat`**. Options like `dateStyle: "long"` or `weekday: "long"` choose what to show. Give a `timeZone` (like `"UTC"` or `"Europe/Lisbon"`) when it matters which clock the time is read on.

```
const when = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 10, 12, 15, 30))
const opts = { dateStyle: "long", timeZone: "UTC" }
console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", opts).format(when))
console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", opts).format(when))
console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { weekday: "long", timeZone: "UTC" }).format(when))
```

Shortcuts do the same in one call: `n.toLocaleString("en-US", options)` and `date.toLocaleDateString("en-GB", options)`. Keep numbers as numbers in your data, and format them only at the very end, when showing them. And make the formatter once and reuse it, rather than making a new one for every number.

intro.title: Modules: import and export
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Real programs are too big for one file. JavaScript splits them into **modules**: each file is a module, with its own variables that the others can't see, and it chooses what to share with **`export`**. Another file takes what it needs with **`import`**.

```text
// prices.js
export const VAT = 0.2

export function withVat(price) {
  return round(price * (1 + VAT))
}

function round(n) {          // not exported: private to this file
  return Math.round(n * 100) / 100
}
```

```text
// app.js
import { withVat, VAT } from "./prices.js"

console.log(withVat(10))     // 12
console.log(VAT)             // 0.2
// round(1.234)              // ReferenceError: round is not defined
```

Those are **named** exports: you import them by their exact names, in braces. You can rename on the way in with `as`, or take everything as one object with `* as`:

```text
import { withVat as addTax } from "./prices.js"
import * as prices from "./prices.js"

addTax(10)
prices.withVat(10)
```

A module can also have one **default** export, often its main thing, like a class. It is imported **without** braces, under any name you like:

```text
// Cart.js
export default class Cart { … }

// app.js
import Cart from "./Cart.js"
```

A few facts worth knowing. A module's code runs **once**, the first time something imports it; every importer shares the same exports. Imports are read-only: you can't assign to an imported name. Paths start with `./` or `../` for your own files; a bare name like `"react"` means a package. In a web page, a script needs `<script type="module">` to use `import`.

The lesson runner here runs one piece of code at a time, so it can't `import` files. The challenges practise the same ideas with what you can run: objects that group exports, private variables inside a function, and code that reads `import` lines as text, like the tools that bundle modules do.

intro.title: From raw text to a report
intro.bodyMarkdown:
This stage puts the quest together. Most data jobs follow the same **pipeline**: **read** the raw text, **parse** it into values, **check** and clean them, **work out** what you need, and **format** a report for people. Each step is a small function, and each one's output is the next one's input.

The example is a runner's log, as CSV text exported from an app. It has spaces after the commas, a blank line and a bad row (`n/a`):

```text
date, km, minutes
2026-10-03, 5.2, 31
2026-10-05, 8.0, 50

2026-10-08, n/a, 20
2026-10-10, 10.5, 61
2026-10-12, 3.1, 19
```

**Parse** into objects with the right types: numbers as numbers, the date as text (or a `Date`). **Check** each row: here, `km` must be a real number above 0. `Number("n/a")` is `NaN`, and `Number.isFinite` catches it. Keep the bad rows aside so you can report them rather than silently drop them.

**Work out** the answers with the list tools you know: totals with `reduce`, the best run with a sort, groups by week or month. **Format** last: `toFixed`, `padStart`, `Intl`.

```
const runs = [
  { date: "2026-10-03", km: 5.2, minutes: 31 },
  { date: "2026-10-05", km: 8, minutes: 50 },
]
const pace = (r) => r.minutes / r.km
const totalKm = runs.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.km, 0)
console.log(`${runs.length} runs, ${totalKm.toFixed(1)} km`)
for (const r of runs) console.log(r.date, pace(r).toFixed(2), "min/km")
```

Because every step is a separate function, you can test each on a tiny example, swap the input (a different file, data from a server) without touching the rest, and add a step (say, an output as JSON) at the end.

intro.title: Hard side quest: An invoice maker
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A bike repair shop gets its orders as JSON from its booking app. Build the code that checks an order and prints a neat invoice: line totals, tax, a due date 30 days after it was issued, and money shown properly.

```text
INVOICE 2026-0147               Riverside Bikes
Issued 2026-11-12                Due 2026-12-12

Brake pads          4 × $12.50           $50.00
Chain               2 × $24.99           $49.98
Labour (hours)    1.5 × $40.00           $60.00

Subtotal                                $159.98
Tax 20%                                  $32.00
Total                                   $191.98
```

Money needs care: `0.1 + 0.2` isn't exactly `0.3` in JavaScript, so round each sum to cents with `Math.round(n * 100) / 100`, and format with `Intl.NumberFormat` only when printing. Dates are in `YYYY-MM-DD` text; work on them in UTC so the computer's time zone can't shift a day.
